Fishermen
FISH-er-men
n. pl. (men who take fish for a living; the trade of the first disciples)
From fisher and men. The Authorized Version uses this form once, in Luke's account of the call by the lake of Gennesaret, where the fishermen had gone out of their ships and were washing their nets.

Biblical Definition

And saw two ships standing by the lake: but the fishermen were gone out of them, and were washing their nets. It is the end of a night's work and a failed one. The Lord teaches the people out of Simon's ship and then gives an order that no fisherman would have expected from a carpenter: Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught. Simon's reply contains both the objection and the obedience: Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net. The catch broke the net and filled two ships until they began to sink, and the effect on Simon was not delight but terror: he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord. A display of power in the one area where he was the expert told him who was in the boat. And the commission follows the confession: Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men. They brought their ships to land, forsook all, and followed him. The trade was not discarded but transposed — the same patience, the same nets, the same deep water, aimed now at men.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one whose occupation is to catch fish; in Scripture, the trade of Simon, Andrew, James and John before the call.

expand to see more

FISHERMAN, n. One whose occupation is to catch fish.

NET, n. An instrument for catching fish and fowls, or wild beasts, formed with twine or thread.

DRAUGHT, n. The act of drawing a net; the quantity of fishes taken by once drawing the net.

CALL, v.t. To invite or summon; in theology, to invite to enter into the kingdom of God.

DISCIPLE, n. A learner; a scholar; one who receives or professes to receive instruction from another.

Key Scripture

Luk 5:2 — "And saw two ships standing by the lake: but the fishermen were gone out of them, and were washing their nets."

Luk 5:4 — "Now when he had left speaking, he said unto Simon, Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught."

Luk 5:8 — "When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord."

Luk 5:10 — "And so was also James, and John, the sons of Zebedee, which were partners with Simon. And Jesus said unto Simon, Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men."

Modern Corruption

Calling is spoken of as the discovery of a personal passion, when Scripture presents it as a summons from outside a man that interrupts the work he was already doing and often contradicts his expertise.

expand to see more

The modern vocabulary of vocation runs inward: find what you love, follow it, and the world's need will meet you there. Luke 5 runs the other way. Simon was doing what he loved and was good at, had just failed at it all night, and received an instruction that his professional judgment contradicted. The call comes from the Lord standing in the boat, and the word the New Testament uses for it is a summons. Amos was following a flock, Matthew was sitting at the receipt of custom, Paul was on the Damascus road doing the opposite of God's will. Not one of them found his calling; each was called.

The order of events in the chapter is also doctrine. The miracle exposes Simon to himself, the confession follows — Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord — and only then comes the commission and the promise. Conviction of sin is not a gloomy preliminary that mature Christians grow out of; it is how a man learns who is in the boat with him. And the Lord's answer to a man asking him to leave is Fear not, and a life's work.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek halieus (G231), a fisherman; diktuon (G1350), a net; zogreo (G2221), to take alive, to catch men.

expand to see more

Greek halieus (G231) — a fisherman; from hals, the sea.

Greek diktuon (G1350) — a net for fishing; were washing their nets.

Greek agra (G61) — a catch, a draught of fish; let down your nets for a draught.

Greek zogreo (G2221) — to take alive, to capture for life; thou shalt catch men.

Greek epistates (G1988) — a master, a commander; Master, we have toiled all the night.

Usage

"“the fishermen were gone out of them, and were washing their nets” — the single occurrence."

"“nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net” — obedience against expertise."

"“from henceforth thou shalt catch men” — the trade transposed."
